title: Can a supplied Karp–Rabin fingerprint be verified in near-linear time?
formal: Given a string $S\in\{0,\ldots,\sigma-1\}^{n}$ and a prime $q$, with $\sigma,q\le n^{O(1)}$, define $h_q(x_1\cdots x_\ell)=\sum_{t=1}^{\ell}x_t\sigma^{\ell-t}\bmod q$. Can one decide in $O(n\log n)$ time whether there exist equal-length substrings $A,B$ of $S$ such that $A\ne B$ but $h_q(A)=h_q(B)$? The modulus is part of the input and cannot be replaced. The deterministic decision problem is the precise target here; the source also permits randomized certification that never accepts a colliding modulus and rejects a collision-free one only with small probability.
why: I include this because it separates fast probabilistic equality tests from fast certification of the hash itself. Near-linear verification of a supplied modulus would make a common assumption in string data structures checkable at nearly the cost of reading the input, while clarifying which composite-fingerprint workarounds are actually necessary.

title: Can LZ77 random access use linear compressed space and logarithmic query time?
formal: Given the greedy LZ77 parse with z phrases of a string $S[1..N]$ over an integer alphabet of size at most N, is there a deterministic word-RAM data structure using O(z) words in total that returns S[i] for any $1\le i\le N$ in worst-case O(log N) time? Words have $\Theta(\log N)$ bits. A phrase is a new literal or a longest prefix of the unparsed suffix having an occurrence starting earlier in S; overlapping copies are allowed. Space includes the stored parse and all query-support information. The uncompressed string is unavailable at query time.
why: I include this because compression is most useful when a small representation remains usable for selective queries. This question asks whether an extra logarithmic storage cost is an inherent price of navigating repeated data or a consequence of converting to a more convenient representation.

title: Can pattern matching run in linear time in the LZ77 input size?
formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm that, given a valid LZ77 representation of z phrases of a text T of length N and an explicit nonempty pattern P of length m, decides whether P occurs contiguously in T in O(z+m) worst-case time? title: Are splay trees dynamically optimal?
formal: Fix n ordered keys and an access sequence X. In the root-BST model, an access is served by rotations until its key is at the root; its cost is one plus the number of rotations. Let OPT(X) minimize total cost over offline executions, allowing an optimal initial tree. Is there a universal constant C such that, for every initial splay tree T₀ and every X, $\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{splay}}(X;T_0)\le C(\mathrm{OPT}(X)+n)$? The additive term allows an arbitrary initial configuration.
why: It asks whether a simple local adjustment rule can match every legal strategy with complete knowledge of the future. The issue is fundamental to instance-sensitive data structures: success would replace a growing competitive penalty by a constant for all access patterns. A counterexample would identify a limitation of splaying that its many separate locality guarantees fail to reveal.

title: Can lazy B-tree priority queues keep their I/O bounds with stable handles?
formal: Is there a deterministic comparison-based external-memory priority queue with a universal constant c of internal storage at most cB words that satisfies the following bounds for every capacity $N\ge B\ge2$? Starting empty and never holding more than N elements, it uses $O(1+N/B)$ external blocks, supports insertion and handle-based decrease-key in $O(1+\log_B\log_B N)$ worst-case I/Os, and supports extract-min in $O(1+B^{-1}\log_2 N+\log_B\log_B N)$ amortized I/Os. Every handle remains valid until its element is removed. All handle maintenance and lookup costs count. Each logarithm is truncated below at one.
why: I include this because stable object identity is part of a data structure’s interface, and its cost can conflict with the locality that makes external-memory algorithms fast. The target is specific enough to attack with a representation or a lower bound, while the obstruction also matters for other structures that move records in blocks.

title: The online Boolean matrix–vector multiplication conjecture
formal: Given a Boolean matrix $M\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}$, receive vectors $v_1,\ldots,v_n\in\{0,1\}^n$ one at a time. Output each Boolean product $(Mv_t)_i=\bigvee_{j=1}^{n}(M_{ij}\wedge(v_t)_j)$ before receiving $v_{t+1}$. Is there any constant $\varepsilon>0$ and randomized algorithm with total running time $O(n^{3-\varepsilon})$ and error probability at most $1/3$? The OMv conjecture asserts that there is no such algorithm. In this formulation the total includes preprocessing of $M$.
why: I include this because it is one of the central assumptions used to explain why many dynamic data structures resist fast updates and queries simultaneously. Refuting it would invalidate a large collection of conditional barriers; proving it would give a major unconditional lower bound for an explicit polynomial-time problem.

title: Do splay trees support deque operations in constant amortized time?
formal: Start from an arbitrary binary search tree containing $n$ ordered keys, and perform $m$ legal double-ended queue operations. Insert-min creates a new minimum as the root with the old tree as its right child; insert-max is symmetric. Delete-min splays the minimum to the root, removes it, and keeps its right subtree; delete-max is symmetric. Is the total number of primitive pointer operations and rotations always $O(n+m)$, with a universal constant? This is Tarjan’s deque conjecture for the specified splay implementation.
why: I include this because it tests whether one general-purpose adaptive representation can recognize a workload whose optimal cost is linear. The remaining gap is tiny numerically but significant mathematically: a proof would explain why expensive local restructuring cannot accumulate across arbitrary alternations of the two ends.

title: Does recursively splitting a splay tree always take linear total time?
formal: Start with an arbitrary n-node binary search tree. A split operation receives a current component tree and a key x in it, searches for x, splays x to that component’s root, and deletes x, leaving its left and right subtrees as separate components. Is the total cost of every legal sequence of n splits O(n)? Count all searches, rotations, and constant-time component bookkeeping. The input to each operation supplies the component’s root handle; identifying which component contains x is not a separate search problem.
why: I include this because recursive partitioning is a basic way to organize ordered data. The conjecture asks whether splaying pays only for the number of objects eventually removed, regardless of the partition order. It is a sharply delimited test of the amortization techniques used for adaptive search trees.

title: Does splaying every BST preorder take linear total time?
formal: Is there an absolute constant C such that, for every n and every two binary search trees A and B on the same n distinct ordered keys, searching for the keys of preorder(B), in order, using bottom-up splaying starting from A costs at most Cn? why: I include this as a concrete test of whether a local restructuring rule detects global order in requests without being told that order. It isolates a major obstacle in understanding adaptive search trees while avoiding the full freedom of arbitrary repeated-access sequences.

title: Does the smallest grammar problem admit a constant-factor approximation?
formal: Do there exist an absolute constant C and a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, for every explicit nonempty string s, outputs an acyclic context-free grammar generating exactly s whose size is at most $C g^*(s)$? There is one production per nonterminal, one designated start nonterminal, and every right-hand side is a nonempty string of terminals and nonterminals. The dependency graph on nonterminals must be acyclic. Grammar size is the sum of all right-hand-side lengths, and $g^*(s)$ is the minimum such size. The alphabet is part of the input, encoded by integer symbols in {1,...,|s|}.
why: This is a fundamental compression-versus-optimization question: can an efficient procedure recover a representation within a fixed factor of the best hierarchical description? It also supplies a benchmark for compressed-data algorithms, whose costs often depend on grammar size rather than on the original string length.

title: Do pure pairing heaps support O(log log n) amortized decrease-key?
formal: For the pure pairing heap defined below, is there a universal constant C such that every legal sequence of M operations starting with empty heaps costs at most $C[M+D(1+\log N)+K(1+\log\log(N+2))]$? Here D counts delete-min operations, K counts decrease-key operations, and $N\ge2$ is the maximum of 2 and the total number of live items across all heaps at any moment. The allowed operations are make-heap, insert, find-min, meld, decrease-key, and delete-min. Count comparisons and pointer-machine steps; keys are distinct opaque values in a totally ordered set, compared at unit cost. Handles to the affected items and heaps are supplied.
why: This is a precise opportunity to separate an analysis gap from a structural limitation of a simple data structure. Priority-queue costs propagate into graph algorithms, and the problem tests how little explicit balancing information is sufficient for optimal amortized behavior.
